At dawn, the harbor wore a coat of silver, and every gull seemed to be holding an argument with the wind. Mara stood at the end of Pier Nine, watching fishing boats return through the mist. Their engines sounded like thunder, or perhaps like the heartbeat of a city waking. She had arrived before sunrise, carrying a paper bag, two train tickets, and the unquiet certainty that some journeys begin only after you stop searching for a destination. The tide crept toward her shoes. She did not move. Somewhere behind her, a shutter lifted, then lowered, and light blinked awake.

By seven, cafés along the quay opened their doors, releasing the smells of bread, coffee, and tomatoes. Mara bought a cup of tea she had no intention of drinking. The woman behind the counter recognized her, though Mara had seen her before. “You have the look of someone waiting for bad news,” the woman said. “Or good news.” “Both wear the same coat,” Mara replied, though she had invented that phrase as she spoke. Outside, a boy balanced a box of lemons on his head and hurried downhill toward the water. The lemons trembled beautifully, impossible fruit precariously pursuing gravity.

An hour later, Mara found a bench facing the sea. She opened the paper bag. Inside were three letters, each written by a different hand. The first was from her brother, formal and brief, explaining that their father had sold the house. The second contained photographs of a garden she remembered only as a blur of green. The third had no greeting, no signature, and one sentence: “Meet me beneath the clock tower when the rain stops.” Mara read it twice. Then she folded three letters along their creases, as if paper could repair itself by being handled with care.

At noon the rain began, patiently, one drop after another, until the harbor dissolved into a field of trembling gray. Mara watched people scatter beneath awnings and clutch newspapers over their heads. She opened her umbrella, though its ribs had bent during the journey. It opened inside out. She laughed, and the sound startled a pigeon from the rail. “Weather,” said an elderly man beside her, “has no talent for subtlety.” Mara handed him the third letter. He read it, frowned, and pointed toward the station clock beyond the rooftops. “It has stopped raining there,” he said, “though only for the moment.”

Mara thanked him and walked toward the station. The streets narrowed, their stones shining like dark mirrors. She passed a bakery displaying crusty loaves, a music shop playing a violin without accompaniment, and a laundromat breathing warm clouds through its doorway. At every corner, the clock appeared in a different disguise: painted on a wall, carved into stone, reflected in a pharmacy window. Each showed a different time, yet all seemed to agree on the hour. Mara checked her watch. It had no hands. She remembered buying it at a railway kiosk, though she could not remember paying for it.

Near the station entrance stood a case containing timetables from decades that no longer existed. Destinations had been scratched away, their passenger routes swallowed by time. Yet one heading remained: OSTRIA, 6:15. Mara touched the glass. A porter emerged from the shadows, wearing a cap embroidered with thread. He studied her face as though reading a ticket. “You are late,” he said. “For what?” Mara asked. “The rain stopped three hours ago.” He unlocked a cabinet and placed a key on the counter. “The clock tower will be expecting you. Take the west platform. Do not board the first train.”

The porter’s key opened a narrow gate at the west platform. Beyond it, a footpath climbed between wet green hedges toward the clock tower above the town. Mara followed, her shoes darkening with every step. Halfway up, she found an abandoned suitcase beneath an oak. Its label bore her name. Inside lay a blue dress, a map of streets she knew, and a photograph of herself beneath the tower. In the picture, she was smiling, older, and holding a key identical to the one in her hand. A breeze shook the branches. Somewhere below, the first train announced its departure.

At the tower, the clock had no face, only a window through which rain fell upward. Mara inserted the key into a door concealed in the stone. It opened onto a staircase. At the top waited a woman in a coat, her hair white as sea foam. “You took the second train,” the woman said. “It was empty.” “I never boarded.” “That is different.” The woman held out her palm. Mara placed the key upon it. The tower began to turn, not physically, but inside Mara, as though the town had changed direction. Below, streets rearranged like threads on a map.

People emerged from doorways, blinking, carrying suitcases toward unfamiliar stations. A child pointed at a house that had been another color that morning. An old fisherman embraced his daughter, asked her name, then wept. Mara watched through the tower’s window. The woman explained that every arrival carried a memory, and every departure returned one. “Did I sell my father’s house?” Mara asked. “You did not. You stopped waiting for a letter telling you what to feel.” The clock chimed once. Each note unfolded like a door. Mara saw the tickets had changed: childhood lay east, while Tomorrow waited far north.

Mara placed the key between the clock’s hands. The woman smiled. “One train will carry you north,” she said. “One will carry you east. Choose.” Mara thought of the house, the letters, the rain, and the kindness of strangers. She chose north. As she descended, the town settled into its shape, and roads sighed with relief. At the platform, an engine waited. The porter removed his cap. “Miss Mara,” he said, “your seat is ready.” Mara boarded, opened the window, and watched the harbor shrink to a shining coin. Beyond the clouds, a bell rang, and she knew the sound of tomorrow.
